analysis.one_liner: Taxes U.S. companies' profits from factories moved abroad to dodge U.S. taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, after drawing 1 sponsor and 6 cosponsors out of 435 House members.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended a tax break that lets U.S. companies put off paying U.S. tax on profits earned by manufacturing subsidiaries set up in countries offering special tax holidays, or in low-cost "runaway plants" abroad that sell goods back into the U.S. Its stated purpose was to discourage companies from moving factories overseas to avoid Federal taxes. It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. manufacturing workers and ordinary taxpayers benefit. By taxing the offshore profits of "tax holiday" and "runaway" plants right away instead of letting companies defer the tax indefinitely, the bill would have removed the tax reward for moving factories out of the United States [S2] [S3]. Domestic manufacturers competing against goods made in tax-holiday plants and sold in the U.S. would also gain a fairer footing [S3], and the Treasury would collect revenue that currently goes untaxed while profits sit offshore.

how_it_helps.text: Adds the profits of foreign subsidiaries that make goods in tax-holiday plants or runaway plants to the U.S. shareholders' taxable income each year, ending the rule that lets those profits go untaxed until brought home.

The bill's stated purpose is to discourage domestic corporations from setting up foreign manufacturing subsidiaries in order to avoid Federal taxes — that is, to remove the tax incentive to move factories and jobs abroad.

The 'runaway plant' definition covers foreign facilities that sell at least 10% of their output in the United States while paying an effective foreign tax rate below 90% of the U.S. rate, so U.S. manufacturers competing against those imported goods would face rivals no longer subsidized by an American tax deferral.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-based multinational corporations with manufacturing plants in low-tax foreign countries would bear the cost: they would owe U.S. tax currently on the profits of those subsidiaries instead of deferring it indefinitely [S3]. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices or to foreign plant workers through reduced investment. Tax-haven governments that use tax holidays to attract factories would lose their main inducement [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals with factories in low-tax countries

drawbacks.text: The 'runaway plant' test is extremely broad: any foreign factory paying an effective tax rate below 90% of the U.S. rate that sells just 10% of its output in the U.S. would qualify. That captures nearly every industrial country, not just true tax havens, so it could tax ordinary foreign operations and leave U.S.-based multinationals paying tax twice — once abroad, once at home — while foreign-headquartered competitors pay only local tax.

The bill grandfathers existing plants: no facility counts as a tax holiday or runaway plant based on money invested before the bill's enactment, so companies that had already moved production offshore would escape the tax entirely.

Raising the tax on offshore manufacturing profits could lead companies to raise prices on goods sold in the U.S. or to shift investment to foreign-headquartered rivals instead of returning production to America.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying problem was real: U.S. tax law let companies indefinitely defer tax on profits from factories moved to low-tax countries, which rewarded offshoring jobs and drained revenue [S3]. But the bill's design was clumsy — its 90%-of-U.S.-rate test swept in nearly every country, and it grandfathered all plants that already moved [S3] — and it never was refined, because it never got a hearing. The larger cost to the public is that the offshoring tax incentive it targeted remained fully intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the Foreign Subsidiary Tax Equity Act on May 24, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law.
Six Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors, but no further action was ever taken on the bill.
The bill was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never voted on; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinationals with factories in low-tax foreign countries are better off, because they kept the right to defer U.S. tax on those offshore manufacturing profits and the tax incentive to move production abroad stayed in place.

for.name: James A. Traficant Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax profits from tax-holiday and runaway foreign plants and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded; all 7 House supporters on record (1 sponsor, 6 cosponsors) were Democrats, and the Democratic-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational manufacturers with offshore plants
industries.note: These companies currently defer U.S. tax on profits from foreign manufacturing subsidiaries in tax-holiday countries; the bill would tax those profits right away, removing the tax reward for moving production offshore. Their interest in keeping the deferral runs against workers and taxpayers who bear offshoring and lost revenue.
Countries that offer tax holidays to lure U.S. factories would lose their main inducement, since profits earned under those holidays would become taxable to the U.S. parent's shareholders.

industries.industry: U.S. domestic manufacturers competing with imports
industries.note: Producers competing against goods made in low-tax foreign plants and sold in the U.S. would no longer face rivals whose offshore profits enjoy an American tax deferral.
